title: XSS and Output Encoding
description: Understand how Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets attackers run malicious scripts in your users' browsers. Learn output encoding, input sanitization, and defense-in-depth strategies using .NET and JavaScript.

data.text: Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS, is one of the oldest and most common web vulnerabilities. It occurs when an application accepts untrusted input and includes it in a web page without proper validation or escaping. The browser then treats that input as executable code, giving an attacker full control over the page for that user.

data.title: XSS categories
items: **Stored XSS**: The malicious script is saved on the server (in a database, comment field, or profile) and served to every user who views it.
**Reflected XSS**: The script comes from the current request — often in a URL query parameter — and is reflected back in the response without encoding.
**DOM-based XSS**: The vulnerability lives entirely in client-side JavaScript. The browser never sees the attack in the HTTP response; the script is inserted into the page by JavaScript itself.

terms.definition: Malicious script persists on the server and executes whenever the infected page is viewed.
Malicious script comes from the request and is immediately returned in the response.
Malicious script is inserted into the page by client-side JavaScript, often via innerHTML or document.write.
Converting special characters into their safe HTML entity equivalents before rendering them in a page.

data.title: Vulnerable Razor template
data.content: This Razor Page directly renders user input without encoding, creating a reflected XSS vulnerability.

data.title: Razor auto-encodes — but not everywhere
data.text: Razor Pages and MVC views automatically HTML-encode expressions like @Model.Query. The danger appears when developers use @Html.Raw(), string concatenation in JavaScript, or innerHTML in JavaScript. Trust the framework's default encoder and avoid bypassing it.

The strongest defense is **context-sensitive output encoding**. The same character needs different treatment depending on where it appears. Inside an HTML element body, encode `<` and `>` as `<` and `>`. Inside an HTML attribute, also encode quotes. Inside JavaScript strings, use Unicode escaping or JSON serialization instead of string concatenation.

data.title: Safe JavaScript rendering in Razor
data.content: Use JSON serialization to inject data safely into a script block rather than string concatenation.
data.code:
<script>
  const searchQuery = @Html.Raw(JsonSerializer.Serialize(Model.Query));
  console.log('Searching for:', searchQuery);
</script>
<!-- JsonSerializer.Serialize escapes quotes, newlines, and <script> -->

data.text: When your application allows users to submit formatted content — like a blog editor or comment box — you need to keep some HTML tags while stripping dangerous ones. The safe approach is to use a well-maintained sanitizer library with a strict allowlist, never a blocklist. Blocklists fail because attackers can invent new tags or bypass filters with creative encoding.

data.title: Sanitizing HTML in JavaScript
data.content: Use the DOMPurify library to clean user-generated HTML before inserting it into the page.

items.text: Use context-sensitive output encoding everywhere you render user data.
items.hint: Different contexts (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL) need different encoding rules.

items.text: Avoid Html.Raw() and innerHTML unless the content has been sanitized.
items.hint: These methods bypass the browser's built-in protections.

items.text: Use a strict allowlist sanitizer for any rich-text input.
Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) as a defense-in-depth layer.
items.hint: A strict CSP can block injected scripts even if encoding fails.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: XSS lets attackers run scripts in victims' browsers by injecting malicious input.
Stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS all require output encoding to prevent.
Use context-sensitive encoding: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, and URL contexts each need different treatment.
A strict Content Security Policy adds a powerful second layer of defense.
data.takeaway: Encode by default, sanitize by exception, and never trust user input.
